title: Maine's $300 Million Salmon Farm Paused, Blaming Trump's Tariffs
summary: Millinocket, Maine, was a thriving paper mill town until Great Northern Paper shut down in 2008. Its abandoned, fenced-off property has sat empty ever since, and the town of 4,100 has struggled. Then came a plan: a $300 million aquaculture venture, backed partly by Norwegian investors, to repurpose the old mill's giant lagoons into a salmon farm called Great Northern Salmon. "It was a marriage made in heaven," said Gail Fanjoy, president of the local chamber of commerce. "Out of the gate, they were going to employ 50 people. That's a home run." The project was about 80 percent toward completion when the company announced last month it was pausing indefinitely, blaming uncertainty caused by the Trump administration's tariffs. Much of its salmon farming equipment was to be imported from Canada. "That was a huge, huge, huge blow," Fanjoy told CBC News. "The Norwegian investors just said, 'We're done, we just can't deal with this.'" Fanjoy, a lifelong resident, doesn't buy Trump's claim that tariffs will revive manufacturing in places like Millinocket. "It's a fallacy," she said. "Paper companies all up and down the Penobscot River and the state of Maine closed, went bankrupt, and a tariff is not going to bring them back." Maine does $6 billion in annual two-way commerce with Canada — significant for a state less populous than Manitoba. The trade war is playing out during a tight U.S. Senate race. Republican Sen. Susan Collins has held her seat for 30 years in a state that hasn't voted for a GOP presidential candidate since 1988. If Democrats want a Senate majority in the Nov. 3 midterms, Maine is a seat they likely need to flip. Tim Woodcock, a Bangor lawyer and Collins backer, said many businesses have been hurt by tariffs on Canadian products. "These two economies are deeply intertwined," he told CBC News. Asked if tariffs could hurt her re-election, Collins avoided the question: "I'm much more concerned about the impact on the people of Maine in general. Many of our products, whether it's blueberries or potatoes or timber or lobster, are harvested here but processed in Canada." She added, "Canada's our friend, our neighbour, our biggest trading partner," and urged both sides to negotiate.
why_it_matters: The pause shows how a policy decision made in Washington — a tariff — can wipe out jobs in a town thousands of kilometres away, because local economies are now woven directly into international trade. It also shows how those same economic shocks can shape elections that decide who controls Congress.

background_read: Millinocket, Maine (a small town in the northern part of the state), grew up around Great Northern Paper, a mill that was once one of the world's largest paper producers; when it shut down in 2008, the town lost its main employer and has been searching for a replacement ever since.

A tariff is a tax a government charges on goods brought in from another country. The United States and Canada trade under a regional agreement — NAFTA from 1994, replaced by the USMCA in 2020 — which normally keeps most goods between them free of such taxes.

Maine's economy is unusually tied to Canada: the state has fewer people than several Canadian provinces, and its lobster, blueberries, potatoes and timber are often shipped north to be processed — the 'two-way commerce' the article mentions.

The U.S. Senate (the 100-member upper chamber of Congress, with two senators per state) faces midterm elections — votes held halfway through a president's four-year term — and control of the chamber can turn on a single state like Maine, which has not voted for a Republican presidential candidate since 1988.

└─ detail: abandoned, fenced-off mill property; a town of 4,100 still struggling
NEW HOPE: a $300 million salmon farm called Great Northern Salmon
├─ WHO: partly backed by Norwegian investors
├─ WHAT: repurposing the old mill's giant lagoons for aquaculture
└─ JOBS: chamber president Gail Fanjoy — about 50 people 'out of the gate'
TURNING POINT: announcement last month that the project is paused indefinitely
├─ STATED CAUSE: uncertainty caused by the Trump administration's tariffs
└─ DETAIL: much of the salmon farming equipment was to be imported from Canada
├─ LOCAL VIEW: Fanjoy — tariffs will not bring paper jobs back, calling it 'a fallacy'

OPEN QUESTION: can the paused salmon farm be revived if the tariff uncertainty ends?

perspectives.perspective: Positive — tariff supporters and the administration
perspectives.description: Supporters of the tariffs argue that taxing imports pushes companies to buy equipment and build factories at home, which could eventually create American jobs. From their view, a stalled project in one town is short-term pain that may lead to longer-term manufacturing gains.

perspectives.perspective: Negative — Millinocket residents and local business voices
perspectives.description: Gail Fanjoy and lawyer Tim Woodcock say the tariffs punished a town that had already lost its mill, killing a project that was about 80 per cent finished. Fanjoy argues tariffs cannot revive paper companies that went bankrupt for other reasons, and that the two economies are too intertwined to split apart without damage.

Maine's $6 billion in annual two-way commerce with Canada shows how porous the border economy really is: goods are harvested on one side and processed on the other. The timing also matters politically, since the trade war is unfolding during a tight Senate race in a state that has not backed a Republican presidential candidate since 1988.

If the tariff uncertainty eases, the Norwegian investors could restart the salmon farm; if it continues, more cross-border projects may be shelved. Meanwhile the Nov. 3 midterms will test whether voters blame tariffs or the trading relationship for local job losses, and Sen. Collins has urged both sides to negotiate.
